questions.question: What is a Count-Min Sketch?

options.text: A probabilistic data structure for estimating frequency of elements in a stream using sub-linear space

questions.explanation: Count-Min Sketch: estimates frequency counts. Uses d hash functions and w counters per row. Space: O(d × w), independent of stream size. Answers: 'how many times did X appear?' with bounded error.

questions.question: How does Count-Min Sketch update work?

options.text: Hash element with d hash functions, increment counter at each hash position

questions.explanation: Update: for element x, compute h₁(x), h₂(x), ..., hd(x). Increment counter[i][hᵢ(x)] for each row i. O(d) time per update. No need to store the element itself.

questions.question: How does Count-Min Sketch estimate frequency?

options.text: Return the minimum value across all d hash positions for that element

questions.explanation: Query: compute all d hash positions, return min(counter[i][hᵢ(x)]). Why minimum? Collisions only increase counts. Minimum is closest to true count. Never underestimates, may overestimate.

questions.question: What type of error does Count-Min Sketch have?

options.text: One-sided error—can only overestimate, never underestimate

questions.explanation: One-sided error: collisions add to counts, never subtract. Estimated count ≥ true count. Error bound: with probability 1-δ, error ≤ εN where N is total count. Tune ε, δ via width and depth.

questions.question: How do width (w) and depth (d) affect Count-Min Sketch accuracy?

options.text: Larger w reduces error magnitude; larger d reduces error probability

questions.explanation: Width w = e/ε (error magnitude). Depth d = ln(1/δ) (failure probability). Want ε=0.01, δ=0.01? w≈272, d≈5. More space = better accuracy. Trade-off: space vs precision.

questions.question: What is a common use case for Count-Min Sketch?

options.text: Finding heavy hitters—elements appearing frequently in a data stream

questions.explanation: Heavy hitters: find elements with frequency > threshold. Network traffic: detect DDoS sources. Ad clicks: find popular ads. Search queries: trending topics. All with bounded memory.

questions.question: Count-Min Sketch vs hash table for frequency counting: when use CMS?

options.text: When cardinality is huge and approximate counts are acceptable

questions.explanation: CMS advantage: fixed memory regardless of unique elements. Hash table: O(n) space for n unique elements. Billions of unique IPs? Hash table = GB of RAM. CMS = KB with bounded error.

questions.question: Can Count-Min Sketch handle deletions?

options.text: Yes, by decrementing counters, but this can cause underestimation

questions.explanation: Deletions: decrement counters. Problem: if collision occurred, decrementing affects other elements' counts. Can go negative or underestimate. Count-Min-Log and other variants handle this better.

questions.question: What is the space complexity of Count-Min Sketch?

options.text: O(n) where n is stream size

questions.explanation: Space: d × w counters. d = O(log(1/δ)), w = O(1/ε). Total: O(1/ε × log(1/δ)). Key insight: space depends only on desired accuracy, not on stream size or cardinality.

questions.question: How is Count-Min Sketch used in network monitoring?

options.text: To estimate traffic volume per source IP for detecting anomalies and DDoS attacks

questions.explanation: Network monitoring: millions of IPs, can't store all. CMS tracks per-IP packet counts. Detect: DDoS (sudden spike from IP), port scans (many destinations from one source). Real-time, bounded memory.

questions.question: What is the relationship between Count-Min Sketch and Bloom filters?

options.text: Both are probabilistic structures using multiple hash functions; Bloom for membership, CMS for counting
CMS is a type of Bloom filter

questions.explanation: Similarities: multiple hash functions, sub-linear space, one-sided error. Bloom: 'is X in set?' (yes/maybe). CMS: 'how many X?' (count/overestimate). CMS generalizes Bloom to counting.

questions.question: You're processing a stream of 1 billion search queries and need to find queries appearing more than 1 million times. What approach?

options.text: Store all queries in a hash table
Use Count-Min Sketch to estimate frequencies, report queries exceeding threshold

questions.explanation: Heavy hitters with CMS: 1) Update CMS for each query, 2) Maintain candidate set of potential heavy hitters, 3) Query CMS for candidates, report those above threshold. Bounded memory, streaming algorithm.
